Moreover, we found that the photon rapidity density in Cu$+$Cu demonstrates a similar power-law behavior versus charged particle multiplicity observed in Au$+$Au collisions at the same energy.

Our work addresses the Tetrahedron Problem in an $\ell_2$-norm context, specifically asking for the properties of a tetrahedron $ABCDF$ that minimizes the sum of the squares of the distances from points $M$ on edge $AF$. The problem is complex, with even the simplest scenarios involving irrational numbers, but with the introduction of a distance weight normalisation, we are able to derive a complete solution, demonstrating that the minimum distance is indeed proportional to the size of the tetrahedron and providing a complete description of the minimum distance configuration.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the true anti-aliasing effect through multiple render targets. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this research introduces a straightforward anti-aliasing approach utilizing two render targets, thereby eliminating the need for additional complexity. Our innovative technique mimics a composite pipeline consisting of alpha blending and delta masking operations, thereby enabling accurate anti-aliasing rendering. Our findings indicate that utilizing two render targets is an effective and straightforward solution for achieving optimal anti-aliasing results.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy.

Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus generating considerable interest among scientists. We delve into the recent breakthroughs in the study of pulsar halos, including the distinct properties of these sources, identified pulsar halos, theoretical mechanisms underlying their exceptionally slow diffusion, their pivotal roles in investigating cosmic-ray propagation and particle injection, and the implications on the puzzles of excess positrons and the widespread TeV gamma-ray excess. Lastly, we outline the prospective research avenues based on the anticipation of discovering more pulsar halos and carrying out deeper investigations into the brightest sources.

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction rely on automatic vehicle monitoring systems or external weather forecasts.
A new multi-class dataset has been introduced consisting of 4600 images representing five weather conditions, captured using a rear-facing camera.
Each vehicle model has a dedicated dataset captured in various weather conditions over a period of time.
A novel data augmentation technique has been proposed to boost the size of the dataset, thereby improving model accuracy.
Evaluations of Convolutional Neural Networks were conducted on the novel dataset and comparison datasets, MetWeather and CLEVR, to determine the most effective approach.
Results show that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art CLEVR dataset accuracy and outperforms MetWeather in four out of five weather categories.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later.

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility. However, controlling these devices is often challenging, especially in dealing with finger-skeleton actuation, finger-finger interaction, and external loads. To address these control complexities, this work introduces a data-driven approach using the Koopman operator theory. By modeling the dynamics of the gripper with a high-dimensional system, KO theory enables online learning and real-time adaptation. The proposed method is modular, allowing for the inclusion of actuation, finger-interaction, and load effects in the dynamic model. The approach is validated through simulations and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to model high-dimensional nonlinear systems and achieve precise control.

One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods.

High-energy emissions from a compact, ancient object called a Compact Flat Spectrum radio source have been observed. Researchers have discovered a highly energetic outburst in a distant CS source named J2102+6015, specifically located at a high redshift value of 4.575. This observation provides early evidence for a high-speed black hole growth very early in the universe. The estimated mass of its black hole is approximately 10^6 solar masses. The researchers also noted that a massive protogalactic cloud is likely responsible for the observations of high, variable polarization in this source, dating back to 1995.

This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective solutions. Current methods, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, our work explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to inform survival time predictions. Our proposed method, which integrates balanced knowledge from two modalities, has yielded remarkable results on two publicly available datasets, significantly outperforming existing benchmarks and deep learning-based models that rely on a single data source.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift cosmological density perturbations through observed quasar spectra analysis. By leveraging sophisticated simulations of cosmic structure formation, a substantial synthetic dataset of absorption spectra and associated 1D matter densities is generated. With this dataset, a series of machine learning models are constructed to predict matter density power spectra. We achieve reconstruction accuracy of approximately 1% for certain wavelengths while noting a corresponding error increase at higher wavelengths. Furthermore, we investigate the size of datasets required to attain a specified error rate, highlighting the data requirements for a desired level of accuracy. This work lays the groundwork for analyzing the forthcoming large-scale datasets anticipated with future observational facilities.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules connected to Lie algebras of the Weyl type. Firstly, we establish criteria for modules over the Lie algebras $A_n^<(k)$ to be free, and characterise irreducible modules over the Lie algebras $A_2^{>0}(k)$. Additionally, we identify a module over the Lie algebra $A_2^{>0}(k)$ that is cyclic but not irreducible.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement of substantial human-human dialogue data for training these
models. Our proposed method aims to address this issue by introducing role
specification to guide the conversation toward specified roles, thereby enhancing
the overall performance. Role specification enables the system to interact with
specified user types, such as being friendly with children and professional in
dealing with experts. Our open-source dataset, "Role Guided Dialogue", which
comprises 9 categories of roles, was used to train dialoGPT, resulting in a
considerable improvement of 47.16% in our evaluation metric compared to the
baseline. The system's robustness was further demonstrated through an user study,
which yielded a substantial 67.56% positive rating.

The binary black hole merger's aftermath leaves a lasting mark on space-time known as gravitational wave memory, and multiple events create a background of residual disturbance known as the stochastic gravitational wave memory background (SGWMB). Researchers found that this phenomenon can be modeled using the concept of Brownian motion. The strength and distribution of SGWMB are directly tied to the frequency and occurrence rate of binary black hole coalescences, and its power spectral density is proportional to the inverse square of frequency. Unlike the more common gravitational wave background produced by binary black holes, SGWMB's characteristics allow it to span a broader frequency range due to the Brownian motion behavior, and therefore dominates at higher frequencies. Additionally, the cross-correlation effects between different parts of the SGWMB signal are non-negligible, and its magnitude is comparable to the intrinsic fluctuations. The detection of SGWMB relies on observatories like LIGO and Virgo, and multiple such facilities will significantly enhance the detection capabilities by increasing the total observation time.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework offers an explanation for why large particles weren't discovered by the Large Hadron Collider. If this framework involves a universe phase change, it creates an interesting possibility where two major phenomena could occur. Firstly, a phenomenon known as neutrino generation could take place, which requires a peV-scale symmetry breaking. Secondly, the gravity waves produced during the phase transition could contain information about the symmetry breaking process, prompting a search for distinct signatures in upcoming searches for cosmic rays from extreme astrophysical sources. In addition, the black holes created during the phase transition may eventually release vast amounts of energy when they decompose, which could significantly impact outstanding problems in high-energy astrophysics.

A reliable and efficient communication system known as semantic communication aims to minimize data transfer and ensure seamless connectivity to diverse users and services. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, incorporating an emergent signaling game framework with a neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence system that facilitates causal reasoning. To design a context-specific communication language, an alternating maximization algorithm optimizes utility values between the transmitter and receiver. This language enhances the transmitter's message content, and in response, the receiver utilizes causal reasoning to analyze and interpret the transmitted information. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed solution achieves substantial reductions in data volume, up to 90%, and displays adaptability in response to changing environmental conditions.

We present a novel approach to word prediction, grounded in the intuitive concept of linking words semantically. In this model, a word's probability is calculated by considering two key factors: its connection to the current context through Naive Bayes, and its association with hidden themes or ideas. These hidden themes act as intermediate bridges, facilitating semantic word connections. By integrating these influences, the word's overall likelihood is determined. This hybrid method, combining Naive Bayes and latent meaning, enables accurate word forecasting. We demonstrate its effectiveness by applying it to the classic task of the Text Prediction with Goals (TPG) dataset.

Recent advancements in Session-based recommendation systems have gained popularity for providing personalized, real-time suggestions with high recall rates compared to conventional techniques. Recent examples include STAMP and NARM models, which, however, did not perform as expected on Zalando's Fashion-Similar dataset in comparison to a basic collaborative-filtering method. Our proposed strategy targets improving item ranking by leveraging the encoded session information through an attention network and demonstrates the potential through Candidate Rank Embedding in reordering items. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach enhances the state-of-the-art performance on the Fashion-Similar dataset and is compatible with existing SBRS methods, yielding substantial improvements of 26.0% and 11.0% in recall@10 and mean absolute error, respectively when combined with STAMP.

We examine a special type of liquid mixture that contains large particles, these particles behave as single entities when together, forming what's known as a colloidal molecule. We focus on a specific scenario where the fluid is in contact with a plane that has an uneven distribution of heat, this area where the fluid meets is known as the nanoscale equilibrium. Our goal is to discover how the temperature gradient affects the movement, energy levels, and structure of these colloidal molecules. We used computer simulations to investigate this, taking into account the interaction between the molecules and their surroundings. These molecules exhibit distinct behaviors based on their size and temperature gradient differences. In certain situations, they show increased energy levels, while their spatial distribution may not fully reflect their true nature due to an uneven balance of forces. These findings reveal that their movement is not as free as expected, restricted by their large size and the prevailing forces. These research outcomes provide valuable insights for understanding the behavior of larger molecules, such as proteins, and their potential organization through control of temperature gradients.

A thorough approach is outlined to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The proposed methodology comprises three core components: generating an accurate 3D mesh that respects the fracture geometry, solving governing equations using a high-order numerical method, and implementing high-quality algorithms for fracture surface representation. Additionally, a detailed strategy is described to ensure seamless interaction between fractures and optimize computational performance. A demonstrated example illustrates how our method handles multiple fractures in a complex setup.

This study centers on low-energy collision avoidance and maintenance of autonomous drone swarms. Two key issues arise in achieving these goals: (1) determining optimal strategies to temporarily disband the formation to avoid collisions, then reforging it while minimizing energy consumption, and (2) developing methods to maintain a stable formation shape while avoiding run-ins. To address the first challenge, we've devised an algorithm using near-optimal point set registration, allowing the drones to rapidly reassemble in a optimized configuration after avoiding collisions. For constant velocity predictions and limited time-to-collision, we've optimized this approach to reduce time and increase efficiency. To resolve the second problem, we've created a formation maintenance algorithm based on registration, allowing the drones to maintain a stable configuration while tracking targets without disrupting the swarm's shape.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two. We derive the multiplicity of the eigenvalue $-1$, the minimum number of unique eigenvalues, eigenvalue limits, the characteristic polynomial, and bounds for the Seidel energy of a chain graph, which outperform previously proposed energy bounds by Haemers. We also obtain additional spectral characteristics, such as eigenpairs, the characteristic polynomial, and energy bounds, in terms of the graph's parameters, thereby enhancing existing general chain graph results. Notably, we establish that the Seidel energy of a chain graph can be as low as $\frac{n-1}{2}$, which surpasses the previous best bound of $\frac{n-1}{2}+\frac{3}{2}$.

In our investigation, we focus on a mean-field optimal control issue for stochastic differential equations featuring time-delay, which are influenced by fractional Brownian motion with a Hurst parameter exceeding 0.5. Given the fractional Brownian motion's nature, which defies the criteria for being a Markov process or semi-martingale, we resort to the fractional White noise calculus and specialized tools for differentiating functions of measures to establish necessary and sufficient stochastic maximum principles. This approach is further exemplified by two applications, including solving a delayed consumption optimization problem from a cash flow and a linear-quadratic problem under delay constraints.

We've developed a unique, detailed two-parameter set of finite-band Jacobi elliptic potentials that correspond to the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator, seamlessly linking two well-known limit cases, each associated with the absence or presence of elliptic parameters. To thoroughly analyze the Dirac operator's spectrum, we've made connections between periodic/antiperiodic eigenvalue problems for the operator, equivalent tridiagonal operator actions in weighted Hilbert spaces and relevant Heun equation connection issues. This, in turn, ties into four related non-self-adjoint, unbounded tridiagonal operator eigenvalue problems which surprisingly possess real eigenvalues.

RSUs are a vital component in V2X, facilitating communication with users; however, congestion areas are often poorly served due to high data traffic, weak signals, and interference, which can be addressed through the use of vehicle relays. To enhance the network in these situations, we've developed a mathematical model for the two-tier vehicular network, incorporating RSUs, vehicle relays, and mobile users. Our analysis examines the average user data rate, network coverage, interference levels, and system performance. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of vehicle relays on the network and identified the optimal number of vehicle relays required to minimize the network's interference and increase the average user data rate.

Wikipedia's ultimate goal is to provide comprehensive, accurate information to the public. However, the platform faces challenges associated with the rapid dissemination of unverified information. Wikipedia's community-driven editing process allows contributors to modify articles, with some edits reflecting informal knowledge and others introducing misinformation. To address the issue of low-quality articles, Wikipedia introduced a labeling system, allowing administrators to mark articles containing low-quality information. These labels enable editors to identify articles needing attention, facilitating administration and maintenance. Notably, only a limited number of Wikipedia editors have the ability to apply these labels, making the process inefficient at times. Our research aimed to develop an automated system for identifying low-quality articles using Wikipedia data, focusing on uncovering underlying patterns in editing behaviors. Our findings reveal that editors exhibiting certain behavior patterns consistently receive warnings from higher-ranking editors, allowing our model to accurately identify articles in need of labels with 74% accuracy, alongside providing insights into the underlying motivations behind these patterns.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. This is achieved through a zero-shot approach where the distillation model is trained to maximize the similarity between its own soft predictions and those of the black-box model, without requiring the black-box model to be part of a training dataset. Our results show that this method significantly outperforms non-black-box knowledge distillation and that it is resistant to perturbations.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected by the LHCb experiment. The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ branching fraction is estimated to be around 1.10$ \times 10^{-4}$, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ branching fraction is estimated to be around 0.440$ \pm 0.060 \pm 0.033$ $\times 10^{-4}$. The study also provides the first measurement of the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay rate relative to the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay rate, which is found to be 0.417 $\pm 0.062 \pm 0.028$.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces featuring tori with twisted commutative actions. Building on the work of Bunce, Kalau, and Strobl, we generalize their results to include actions on general topological spaces, then use this framework to express the twisted Dirac operator's spectral flow in terms of the T-dualized action, resulting in the establishment of a $C^*$-algebraic equivalence between the twisted union of point spectrum and the union of point spectra of the Dirac operators on the original and T-dual spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the twisted union of point spectrum possesses a natural $C^*$-algebra structure. Using the topological T-dualities constructed from free abelian groups of finite rank equipping tori with actions, we are able to recover known results and the Pimsner-Voiculescu functor providing examples of the twistings.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework that circumvents this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios confirms the efficacy of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, showcasing improved performance and accelerated convergence when compared to traditional reinforcement learning approaches.

This paper proposes a metric-based approach to constructing and analyzing High-Rate Polar Alignment Convolutional codes. The code design is driven by a new metric that optimizes polar alignment, leading to efficient codes with superior error rate performance. The proposed codes have a high rate of transmission and exhibit excellent error-resistance capabilities. The code construction is facilitated by a simplified and more intuitive method to calculate the polar decomposition of a binary convolutional code. This approach is contrasted with a previously established method that relies on the generalized Schur decomposition.

This project tackles the complex problem of simultaneously monitoring the positions and shapes of hands and objects in a sequence of depth point cloud data, starting from the known poses in the initial frame. To achieve this, we introduce a network called HandTrackNet, the first point cloud hand tracking system, to continuously estimate hand keypoints, hand masks, and grasped objects along with their poses in an optimal coordinate system. To address the issue of tracking discontinuities and optimizing hand placement, we leverage a joint template matching regression module. Additionally, a variety of training and evaluation methods are proposed to ensure robust performance across diverse scenarios. Extensive experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach over traditional RGB hand tracking methods and an acoustic-based method for detecting false hand poses. Finally, a set of pre-trained models and tracking results for the MSR HandTrack Benchmark and KIT hand tracking benchmark are made available on our website.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Our system's dependence on minimal processing and rapid image processing enables efficient offline and online training. Through thorough experimentation on diverse scenarios, our method demonstrates superior results and adaptability compared to alternative approaches.

A new model is introduced to describe treatment interference, specifically within social networks structured according to the k-nearest-neighbors (KNN) system. This system categorizes individuals into three groups: those whose treatments fall within the KNN range (interfered with), those whose treatments fall outside this range (non-interfered with), and themselves (the treated individual). Traditional methods for identifying treatment interference involve testing controlled direct effects, but such approaches face limitations when trying to distinguish between interfered-with and non-interfered-with units. To address this issue, a new method is proposed that infers the interference model by examining the local context of treated individuals and testing for significant differences in treatment effects among these categories. Simulation data illustrate the method's effectiveness, particularly in distinguishing between interfered-with and non-interfered-with units. Ultimately, application of this method depends on proper selection of the KNN parameter, achieved by analyzing data or making an informed decision based on knowledge of the studied social network.

Calculations of neutrino emissions from self-interacting Dark Matter particles within a Neutron Star's environment have been conducted, incorporating a specific mediation particle. This mediation particle has a short-range effect and is feeble in neutrino interactions, but is strongly coupled to Dark Matter particles. Within a simplified mediation mechanism, the Dark Matter particle's mass is primarily influenced by a four-derivative operator. As a result, the mediation particle can be seen as a pseudoscalar particle with a long-range effect. Within this framework, the mediation mechanism significantly enhances the production of secondary light Dark Matter particles, leading to enhanced neutrino emissions from Neutron Star Dark Matter particle interactions. Consequently, the mediation mechanism is subject to stricter constraints from Neutron Star observations, particularly in the case of the 580 millisecond pulsar in the NGC 6383 cluster.

The ongoing UNIONS project, the most comprehensive optical survey to date in the Northern sky, has partnered with CFIS for $r$-band data, boasting exceptional seeing of 0.65 arcseconds and complete magnitude 24.5 for precise weak-lensing research. Our analysis covers an expansive 1700 square degrees of the sky, cataloging 30 million galaxies, translating to a density of 6.8 per square arcminute. A low-level systematic bias was found in this research, providing a groundwork for extensive cosmological studies using the UNIONS/CFIS data.

A notable consequence of a particular diophantine equation outcome, known as the Four Multiple Conjugates Theorem, yields an infinite number of real roots for certain polynomial equations of degree two, involving irreducible complex number fields. In the case where the discriminant is positive, these roots can be found in pairs within complex planes, describing horizontal and vertical lines. Building on the ideas of a prior paper, new findings regarding the placement of these roots can be described through an analysis at a finite scale, at a given size $\Lambda$, where the distance between each root in a set of $M$ roots approximates $\Lambda^{-d/(2n)}$. Here, the value of $d$ depends on the dimension of the real number field $k$, equal to $s-1$ or $s-2$ respectively, and $n$ represents the number of conjugate roots. In the scenario where the discriminant is negative, additional rotations, influenced by the angle $\theta$, where the sine of $\theta$ is nonzero, result in a new set of root arrangements, translating the previous scale analysis into a rotated domain. This new understanding leads to an interpretation of an old conjecture regarding certain real number fields, where the size of the roots $\lambda$ within these fields should satisfy the relationship $|y_i\log\frac{q}{\lambda_i}-x_i\log\frac{q}{x_i}| \leq \frac{1}{2} \

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, a specific criterion holds, where k-rationality implies k-Du Bois, which in turn is equivalent to an intersection property for certain ideals. Additionally, for local complete intersections defined over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, we find that k-rationality is equivalent to k-Du Bois. Furthermore, for quasi-self-invariant line bundles on projective varieties, we investigate related non-k-rational singularities.

We've observed the appearance of field-induced Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless correlations in a weakly coupled, spin-1/2 Heisenberg material called [Cu(pz)2(2-HOpy)2](PF6)2. Due to its moderate exchange coupling of about 6.8 Kelvin, the application of laboratory magnetic fields produces a noticeable anisotropy of the spin correlations in an XY plane. This significant BKT regime develops because of a weak interlayer exchange of about one millikelvin that causes 3D correlations as the critical temperature is approached, resulting in an exponential increase in spin-correlation length. Nuclear magnetic resonance, muon spin resonance measurements and inelastic light scattering confirm our findings.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the interplay between axion-like particles, right-handed neutrinos, and sterile dark matter components. The existence of an additional neutrino or an axion-like particle below the TeV mark has found support, and could potentially be probed through experiments like the LHC, BelleII, XENON, and future dark matter detection experiments.

This study optimizes the execution time of established algorithms for classically simulating quantum computations based on stabilizer forms. The research provides upper limits on the maximum number of unique stabilizer gates required within a certain timeframe. Initially, the investigation specifies a maximum number of unique Pauli gates needed to transform a initial state into a target state within a certain time frame. Next, the study generalizes the findings to describe the maximum number of unique Clifford gates required to achieve a similar state transformation. The research utilizes a novel approach to derive these maximums by focusing on the distance between classical and quantum states rather than their associated Pauli matrices. The results indicate a linear relationship between the number of qubits and the number of unique gates required for both algorithms, thereby offering a performance improvement over previous simulations for specific quantum computations.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in a complex quintessence field framework. We first examine the likelihood function for the model's parameters, before determining the range of suitable values. We subsequently analyze solutions in the framework of general initial conditions. We also investigate the asymptotic behavior of solutions, including their application to the complex scalar field. We delve into two specific models, based on a symmetry and charge, and discuss their implications in relation to the model's real application. Finally, we explore the likelihood distribution of the model's parameters in this context.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 41 nights of 46.6 hours of exposure time and a low signal-to-noise ratio of approximately 10. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 182,000 spectra after 121 nights of 125.8 hours of exposure time and a higher signal-to-nonoise ratio of approximately 20. The study allowed researchers to monitor a significant number of objects and provided essential data for additional research in astrophysics and cosmology. Researchers were able to monitor and track 348,794 stars, 1,617,374 candidate variable stars, and further narrowed down the scope of 11,795 objects of interest (AOI). The study also enabled the accurate determination of solar system object velocities, including a total of 286 measurements for 128 objects. Furthermore, the study significantly increased the number of known small-amplitude variable stars and provided data for 1,597 AOI. Researchers were able to identify 1,597 objects of interest (AOI), including a wide range of variable star types, such as RR Lyrae, Delta Scuti, and W Dolph stars. Previous research has suggested the use of SRAM-based TRNGs for extracting entropy from SRAM arrays. As these arrays are commonly employed in microcontrollers for data storage, SRAM-based TRNGs can be easily integrated into existing systems. This work improves upon existing SRAM-based TRNG approaches by enhancing their reliability and security. Specifically, we propose the use of SRAM cells with reduced supply voltage to enhance the extraction of entropy. This is because a lower supply voltage increases the likelihood of bit flips during read operations, effectively generating random data. However, existing SRAM models inaccurately predict bit flip rates, leading to reduced TRNG reliability. To address this, we developed a new model, known as SRAMDEMF, to accurately model bit flip rates in SRAM arrays. Furthermore, we investigated how manufacturing processes can affect TRNG accuracy and identified thermal and electrical variations as primary factors. To improve TRNG reliability, we developed a dual-architecture design featuring a combination of SRAM and flip-flop elements. This dual-architecture design allows users to select between static and dynamic SRAM configurations, effectively addressing existing TRNG reliability issues.

A preliminary design and computational simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm our design's validity, we conducted a theoretical study of two specific molecules, bis-terpyridine-CuII and bis-terpyridine-PdII, demonstrating that they exhibit stable switching behavior at room temperature due to their compact size and planar geometry, allowing for easy integration into nanotechnology applications.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an attractive alternative to conventional methods. By applying loop-tree duality, the Feynman integrands are simplified to a form that only captures physical information, resulting in a causal representation. In this discussion, we explore the application of all-loop causal representation to describe multi-loop Feynman integrands, which can be characterized by loop topological features. To address concerns regarding numerical stability in loop-tree duality-based calculations, we examine case studies involving numerical evaluations of planar and non-planar two-loop triangles under varying kinematic conditions.

This paper aims to broaden the understanding of quantum walks within one-dimensional systems by deriving a specific eigenfunction expansion, specifically tailored for the discrete and continuous time models. We start by establishing the natural modes of the system, which are subsequently used to construct the eigenfunction expansions for the respective operators in both discrete and continuous time models. To validate our approach, we demonstrate the equivalent forms of the eigenfunction expansions for the one-dimensional system, which are comparable to the known operator methods. Furthermore, we successfully applied this approach to derive the explicit eigenfunctions for the one-dimensional system. We also used this method to derive the probability amplitudes for the one-dimensional system, which are expressed as a function of position. These amplitudes are obtained by expanding the Hamiltonian and the initial state within the natural mode basis. We then calculated the probability amplitudes for the one-dimensional system, which are expressed as a function of position, and used these amplitudes to derive the probability amplitudes for any given state in the system. We then compared our results with the probability amplitudes obtained through the standard operator method, finding that they are equivalent. We also used this method to predict the probability amplitudes for the one-dimensional system, which are expressed as a function of position, and used these amplitudes to derive the probability amplitudes for any given state in the system. This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to amplify non-traditional optical phenomena. This insight drives an investigation of the optical characteristics of a system where both the optical cavity and mechanical oscillator undergo $q$-deformation. The study focuses on the optical density of states, photon-photon interaction, and the behavior of tunable optomechanical amplification, enhancement, and isolation within this optomechanical framework. The findings indicate that $q$-deformation enhances the speed and flexibility of observing these optical phenomena. Specifically, for $|q| = 0.5$, the typical optomechanical system can exhibit amplified transmission, isolation, and Dirac points in the phase shift, as well as negative and positive isolation. However, these features heavily rely on the value of $q$.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the energies of these states with those of traditional scissors states.

We examine the feasibility of fabricating and managing electron spins and orbitals in ultrathin metal-oxide films with in-plane lattice parameter $a$ and out-of-plane lattice parameter $c$, utilizing experimental techniques that allow for fine-tuning of $c$.
Utilizing epitaxial growth on different substrates, we identify four unique configurations: (1) compressive strain, (2) expansive strain, (3) nearly isotropic conditions, and (assistant specific lattice mismatch cases which introduce unique anisotropy).
Through these scenarios, the tendency for in-plane electron spin polarization is found to correlate with the out-of-plane orbital polarization, yet opposing effects arise from epitaxial constraints and lattice mismatch.
Consequently, managing spin and orbital interactions in metal-oxide films offers promising potential for generating novel functionality through the manipulation of film strain.

The occurrence of diffusion can be seen across various natural phenomena, and this widespread application is attributed to the broad implications of the central limit theorem. In recent decades, scientists have studied anomalous diffusion, and this may lead to novel phenomena emerging from ordinary processes. Specifically, in this research, a model is presented that describes laser-cooled atoms in an optical lattice as experiencing anomalous diffusion. By combining fractional calculus and random matrix theory, the resulting system exhibits unique characteristics, and this study provides a mathematical framework for modeling and analyzing the processes occurring within the optical lattice. By examining the distribution of atoms in the lattice, scientists can gain insight into the underlying processes, and this model enables the calculation of probability distributions using fractional Fourier series expansions. Our results demonstrate that the probability distributions of atoms in the lattice are Gaussian-like, and this is valid for both large and small numbers of lattice sites, and regardless of the spatial location within the lattice. However, when the number of lattice sites is sufficiently small, the Erben-Duke distribution is observed, and this indicates a transition from the Erben-Duke distribution to the Gaussian-like distribution as the number of lattice sites increases. Additionally, our results also show that the probability of finding atoms at the edge of the lattice follows a \pi/2-shifted Erben-Duke distribution, and this indicates a symmetry difference between the probability distributions of atoms at the edge and the center of the lattice.

This study investigates the effects of information dissemination on cryptocurrency markets. Firstly, a cryptocurrency trading network is defined by employing cryptocurrencies as nodes and weekly log returns linked via Granger causality. The analysis traces its development over time, focusing on the relationships' changes since the launch of the first cryptocurrencies in 2009. Our results show that the trading network initially experienced rapid expansion during the initial phase of cryptocurrency adoption (2009-2017), followed by a slower increase in newly added nodes in the subsequent period (2018-2021). Furthermore, the representation of cryptocurrencies in the trading network was initially driven by cap-driven relationships, but by 2018, other factors began to influence their connectivity. Our time-series analysis of node centrality and edge strength also reveals that the trading network underwent significant changes during the two periods, affecting the positions of various cryptocurrencies in the network. In addition, our findings show that the positive correlation of high-order Granger causality with node centrality in the early phase gradually transitions to a negative correlation in the late phase, indicating that understanding the complex structure of cryptocurrency trading networks is crucial for making informed investment decisions.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial process influencing the formation of clouds, and it predominantly involves the association of one gas molecule at a time. In this process, highly associated water and other molecules tend to oversimplify the system's behavior. In particular, they fail to consider the importance of quantum mechanics, specifically zero-point motion, in determining the reaction rates. In this investigation, we examine the impact of zero-point motion in the formation of small sulphuric acid-water clusters using theoretical methods. In doing so, we used the principle of matched clusters to calculate reaction rates, and compared the results between two different models: one that accounts for the importance of quantum mechanics and another that dismisses it in favor of a more classical approach. In small clusters, the model accounting for the importance of quantum mechanics yielded significantly higher reaction rates. However, this difference diminished in larger clusters, and we attribute this discrepancy to the role of sulphuric acid in facilitating the association, as well as the rising water content in the cluster. In contrast, the model dismissing the importance of quantum mechanics performed better at higher water content, and we suggest that this dismissive model may better represent the processes influencing the primary aerosol particle formation. In total, our investigation underscores the necessity of considering the importance of quantum mechanics in the formation of small sulphuric acid-water clusters.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair, compactifying a perception pair, and compactifying a space of operators invariant under group actions and non-expansive in nature. It's proven that every perception pair with measurements from a totally bounded space and rich enough to impose a metric on their common domain, can be isometrically embedded within a compact perception pair. Similarly, it's proven that the space of non-expansive group invariant operators can be isometrically embedded into a compact space of the same, provided the operators' images form a cover over their codomain, resulting in new compact perception pairs that compactify their original counterparts, which possess totally bounded domains and rich perceptions, thereby facilitating explicit embedding.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this phenomenon in materials that conduct heat in a two-dimensional lattice, researchers found that this analogy doesn't hold perfectly. By calculating a key measure of how the materials react to temperature gradients, researchers discovered that it can't be fully explained by the materials' properties and must be influenced by a topological number. Additionally, even though this topological number does affect the materials' response to temperature gradients, it doesn't seem to follow a expected relationship with the materials' properties. These findings are confirmed through numerical simulations and suggest that there is more to learn about how temperature gradients interact with materials that have these specific topological properties.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a major objective for several methods, including regularization. While regularization is often seen as being external to the model architecture, our research indicates that many model parameters introduce geometric complexity, serving as a form of regularization in deep learning models. We demonstrate that specific neural network layers, such as convolutional and fully connected layers, can be viewed as applying geometric complexity regularization through feature transformation. By reinterpreting certain architectural elements, we uncover additional complexity regulators, such as pooling layers, recursive functions, and encoder-decoder models. This understanding can be leveraged to design more effective complexity regularization techniques in future research.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an only partially resolved issue, with notable practical applications and research implications.  The quality of input data significantly impacts the performance of machine learning models in automated essay grading.  In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of data augmentation through sentence recombination as a technique to enhance automated essay scoring using NLP models based on the Transformer architecture.  The approach of combining sentences, often applied in other NLP tasks, has not been widely explored in the context of automated essay grading.  We compare the performance of different models, including the basic Transformer architecture and variants such as BERT and RoBERTa, on both augmented and non-augmented datasets.  The results show that sentence combination can improve the correlation between the human and automated grades, with the BERT model exhibiting the most significant gains.  A version of the BERT model fine-tuned on both essay pairs and augmented data achieved a high Pearson correlation of 0.884 between human and automated grades, outperforming its baseline counterpart by 0.070.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delimit toric models within our framework, specifically marginal independence models, by allowing liberty in the underlying cones. A key aspect of our research offers a combinatorial solution to identify independence models associated with specific simplicial complexes, sometimes even their sole solution. By analyzing the Markov random fields resulting from our models, we gain insight into their nature and apply our findings to various real-world scenarios, such as coxph models and multiple testing problems.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to improve social mobility. This strategic allocation of opportunities can lead to a more equitable distribution of resources in the long run by reducing income inequality. This positive outcome is achieved by reducing the concentration of wealth among higher socioeconomically situated individuals.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT (DRC). Our implementation is integrated into the Ithaca 2.0 proof of stake blockchain, allowing for the simultaneous use of Delegated Proof of Stake and RingCT technology. In doing so, we add a new layer of privacy to the DPoS network, while also enabling scalable transactions. Furthermore, our research includes a performance comparison of Delegated RingCT with Integrated RingCT, as well as an examination of the effects of hidden zones on transaction processing times and network bandwidth.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons simultaneously produced in high-energy collisions between protons.  These collisions were performed at the CERN LHC with the CMS experiment's data set that contains 137 fb$^{-1}$ worth of information.  Separate searches for individual combinations of bosons, including W boson variations, have been done using several patterns of final particle arrangements.  Together, the signals for these processes indicate a cross-section of boson creation that is slightly larger than that predicted by the standard model, occurring at a rate of about 1.79 times standard model expectations.  Specifically, signals for individual W boson variations have a rate of about 1.25 to 1.62 times standard model expectations.

Previous efforts to create a Universal Dependencies (UD) treebank for Hebrew were hindered by the language's fixed script and non-standard punctuation marks, requiring specialized preprocessing techniques to be incorporated into the UD annotation scheme. These challenges have been addressed, enabling the revival of UD Hebrew treebanking efforts. The newly formed Hebrew Treebank Annotation Team is now preparing a UD annotated corpus based on a diverse range of texts, including news articles, academic publications, and children's books, to represent the language's syntactic structure effectively. The team is also building upon the successes of the first Hebrew UD treebank, which was based on texts from the 1990s and early 2000s, by incorporating modern texts into the new corpus. The total corpus size is expected to exceed 3,000 sentences. The article provides an overview of the motivations behind these new efforts and outlines the approaches being taken to address the unique challenges posed by Hebrew, as well as the potential applications of the UD Hebrew corpus.

We maintain fixed $p \in [1,\infty)$ and $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and a probability measure $\mu$. It is proven that for every $(\mu)$-incompressible subset $M$ of $\ell_p$, there exists an $\varepsilon$-isometric embedding from $M$ into $\ell_p(\mu)$ that relies solely on countably many orthonormal basis elements. This result generalizes an earlier finding from the authors for $\ell_2$. Alternatively, under the additional assumption that $\mu$ is strictly positive, it is possible to achieve an embedding that relies on finitely many basis elements. This result improves upon an independent concurrent one by Bronshtein and Olesenko for $\mu$ being either countable or a finite measure. We prove a sharp sufficient condition for the existence of $(\mu)$-incompressible subsets in $\ell_p$. As a consequence, it is shown that for any $(\mu)$-incompressible subset $M$ of $\ell_p$, there exists an $(\varepsilon+1)$-isometric embedding from $M$ into $\ell_p(\mu)$ that relies solely on countably many orthonormal basis elements.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making cooperative modeling more feasible. As research advances, diverse collaborations can lead to novel methodologies and an accumulation of knowledge, eventually resulting in a wide range of efficient and robust modeling methods. This paper serves as an introduction to current cooperative efforts and their outcomes, providing an overview of cooperative data-driven modeling and its applications, while also highlighting potential obstacles and future areas of exploration.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance potentially unsafe control inputs with safety assurances through constraint satisfaction. This paper presents a refined safety filter design with a proven guarantee of system safety using a methodical approach rooted in system level synthesis. The resulting safety filter module is a predictive control-type system that seamlessly integrates safety requirements. Despite its increased complexity, this module remains scalable and applicable to a wide range of linear safe system models.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics and single photons, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum-state QKD system. Specifically, our research showcases that even partial randomization of the phase can be exploited by a malicious attacker, thereby compromising the entire system. Moreover, our findings also reveal that the same attack method is effective against the decoy-state QKD system, particularly when it utilizes a limited number of real photon pairs. Our intention behind this research is to highlight the potential hazards and stimulate discussions on enhancing the security of QKD systems to prevent quantum hacking.

Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context zero-shot learning abilities with notable success. However, the influence of training data on this capability is still relatively unexplored. To contribute to an understanding of this relationship, we examined the impact of domain-specific datasets on the learning abilities of context-free and in-context models. Notably, our findings indicate that a substantial language model can acquire new abilities through the incorporation of relatively small, domain-specific training datasets, even when these domains are not supported in its initial 13 billion parameter pretraining. More interestingly, our research uncovered two counterintuitive phenomena: (1) pretraining on a domain can sometimes hinder the model's in-context learning ability within that domain; (2) there often exists a certain amount of training data required for in-context learning to occur. To further investigate these observations, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between training data, lexical coverage, and in-context learning performance, uncovering several key insights. Ultimately, our research offers practical guidance for selecting domain-specific training datasets for large language models.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central nebulae, yet little is known about what happens when the initial, granular phase of cooling occurs in the core. Employing simulations for the first time to capture this entire process, our research reveals that cold clouds form and then either expand or break apart based on the strength of thermal conduction, magnetic fields, and the rate of radiative cooling. When the cooling process is highly efficient and magnetic fields are weak, large, dense clouds form that can weigh as much as millions of solar masses. In contrast, low rates of cooling result in the creation of smaller, more dispersed structures. Conversely, strong magnetic fields cause the material to spread out, preventing high-mass cloud formation, regardless of the cooling rate. This is because magnetic fields suppress the contraction by exerting an outward pressure, allowing material to spread and reduce the local density below the threshold required for high-mass cloud formation. Furthermore, a sudden increase in thermal conduction can lead to the destruction of emerging clouds, resulting in the creation of a diffuse, low-density halo. This is particularly true at low cooling rates, where the clouds are already weak and easily destroyed by a small increase in thermal conduction. The results of our simulation align with the findings of the Chandra X-ray telescope observation of the Perseus cluster, which shows a sharp boundary between the core and the main cluster body. The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty- and charm-hadron decays serves as
a crucial test of the Standard Model's predictions, also acting as a sensitive
indicator to uncover physical phenomena not accounted for within the SM. The
presentation includes precise measurements of observables connected to the
unitary triangles stemming from unitarity constraints on the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-
Maskawa matrix describing quark mixing, alongside recent $C\!P$ violation
measurements in beauty- and charm-hadrons. Specific emphasis is given to an
analysis that initially identified direct $C\!P$ violation in beauty baryons and
two analyses that made precise predictions on the strength of the effective
weak interaction responsible for quark mixing.

New calculations of bosonic scattering amplitudes in superstring theory have been conducted for processes such as $VV\to VV$, $TT\to TT$, and $TV\to TV$. These calculations used a newly developed off-shell formulation of the bosonic superstring theory. The amplitudes were computed using a novel technique involving a worldsheet correlation function in a specific conformal field theory. The calculated amplitudes are found to be consistent with an established formula proposed by Gross. The calculations also reveal a surprising connection to a string field theory framework, where the amplitudes can be expressed as derivatives of a geometric object called S-matrix. The calculations provide strong evidence for the validity of the Gross formula in superstring theory.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we can synchronize computation with data collection and balance resource allocation with energy harvesting. Our approach also involves utilizing edge AI for decision-making, which allows for intelligent and efficient management of heterogeneous resources. Based on these strategies, we've developed two optimization methods for running online simulations quickly, focusing on sustainable resource management. Numerical results show that these methods significantly reduce power consumption and maintain high data quality compared to traditional methods.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a vocabulary-independent speech system without transcription data, requiring the transformation of training data into acoustic units for test synthesis. This study explores identifying and modeling the fundamental acoustic units in speech, comprising both transient and steady-state regions. The transient regions are equivalent to consonant-vowel and vowel-consonant units, while steady-states include sonorants and fricatives. The speech signal is first segmented into CVC-like units based on a short-term energy contour and then grouped using graph clustering. The clustered units are initialized to include transient onset and decay segments and steady-state regions of varying lengths, and their representations are refined through self-supervised learning and unsupervised data imputation. The proposed approach is demonstrated on TTS datasets, and the effectiveness of the method in terms of similarity to human speech is evaluated using metrics like mean absolute error and frequency feature correlation.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion under posture and force constraints poses a challenging nonlinear optimization issue, often accompanied by extensive computation times. We've developed a multi-step optimization method incorporating data-driven linkages between stages to tackle these nonlinearities efficiently. Both cluster analysis and evolutionary strategies are applied to determine the specific parameters of McCormick envelope relaxations, allowing us to leverage learned constraints across preceding stages, thus yielding better performance, faster solution times, and more interpretable results. Our planner was thoroughly tested and validated through a variety of experiments on a quadruped robot, demonstrating its capacity to optimize its gait while maintaining stability and contact with diverse terrains.

We have developed a concise method to determine the minimum number of operations required to transform one quantum state into another, under specific constraints such as fixed basis and continuous measurements. Our method relies on two key concepts - the quantity of a state within a particular basis and the degree of its overlap with another basis. We show that these two values can be manipulated using local operations, effectively enabling us to establish strict limits on the number of operations needed to achieve specific outcomes, including maximal overlap and continuous measurements. Notably, we discovered that some states are optimally converted by measurements that are not necessarily complementary, contrary to previous assumptions. Furthermore, we used our approach to set lower bounds on the number of operations required for tasks like quantum compression and quantum cloning, while also proving that certain protocols are indeed optimal, thereby confirming previously conjectured outcomes.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines characteristics of a planar nonlinear pendulum. This model was subject to two types of excitation - parametric in the vertical plane and a combination of parametric and direct in the horizontal plane. The position of the pivot changed over time, inducing these excitations. In the scenario of vertical excitation, the averaging method helped to establish stability boundaries for two steady-state solutions, whereas vertical and horizontal excitations led to system resonances identified through multiple scale methods, with results validated using exact numerical integration techniques.

In our research paper, we address a challenge in decentralized machine learning by developing a new algorithm that accommodates varying data conditions among network nodes. The existing decentralized learning algorithms assume homogeneous data conditions, which might not hold in real-world applications. Our proposed DR-DSGD algorithm overcomes this limitation by incorporating a robustness term into the regularized empirical risk minimization problem, allowing each node to optimize its model via stochastic gradient descent method. We leverage the concept of Wasserstein distance to measure data discrepancies and transform it into a manageable optimization problem. Utilizing regularization and convexity, we establish a strong performance guarantee for our algorithm. Moreover, we conduct extensive experiments to validate our algorithm's efficacy.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth model of energy release, our findings demonstrate that entropy generated before equilibrium is established naturally accounts for the common trend of decreasing particle production with increasing centrality observed in nucleus-nucleus collisions. Additionally, we calculate the energy density of the initial state and outline potential avenues for future research.

Using complex simulations of star-forming clouds, the process of how high-velocity jets form and maintain slower-moving outflows is being examined. The equations used in the simulations include magnetic fields and the forces of adiabatic gas movement, but not the influence of outflow velocity or direction. The simulations show that high-velocity jets can only be sustained for a short time if they are constantly fed by jets with higher velocities. If this is not the case, the jets quickly fade. Furthermore, even if the high-velocity jets are prolonged, they do not appear to explain how low-velocity outflows are maintained. An alternative explanation is that low-velocity outflows are actually small, high-velocity jets that have been diluted by their surroundings, taking on lower velocities as a result.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures system safety in the presence of destabilizing influences, such as saturation and filter error. This framework is applied to a two-degree of freedom mechanical system with a compromised actuator and multiple integrated filters (MIFs), yielding numerical results that demonstrate its effectiveness.

This research project seeks to offer fresh perspectives on how gravitational influences affect an object orbiting the Earth, specifically considering its model as a perfect sphere with no other gravity influences at play. By incorporating the object's mass and radius, as well as accounting for the Sun's gravity, we establish a mathematical model that describes the object's equilibrium positions. These positions are analyzed in relation to various orbital configurations around the Earth. Due to the complexity of these orbits, which are influenced by a combination of libration periods, we utilize numerical simulations in addition to analytical modeling to gain insights. Our study covers a range from very close to very distant orbits, spanning from 0 to 400 million kilometers. This extensive scope allows us to discover new resonances and explore their characteristics in detail.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to one-dimensional and two-dimensional paradigms, specifically the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and a model of hollow-core phonon modes. The results show that the dipole-based model is gauge invariant, yielding the same results as the velocity-based model despite differences in their precisions. The dipole-based model offers computational benefits, especially in its treatment of periodic domains.

In a problem setting called category-level perception, we aim to identify objects within a specific group (like cars or dogs) based on key landmark points and their 2D or 3D positions. This approach offers efficient object detection in less-than-ideal conditions, as it focuses solely on identifiable characteristics rather than low-level image details. Our research involves developing accurate PPE algorithms for both 2D-LVE and 3D-LVE tasks, where we use simulated data to train and test models, with real-world data providing additional validation. Our model, PKE, demonstrates exceptional performance in PPE tasks by effectively utilizing semantic keypoints, mapping them to optimized object shapes, and accounting for potential detection errors through uncertainty quantification. PKE achieves remarkable results, with a few notable highlights including state-of-the-art PPE outcomes, the ability to provide reliable object class predictions with low variability, and the capacity to efficiently operate on resource-constrained devices like Raspberry Pis, even when resource availability is limited.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses Bayesian statistics to optimize sample size and allows information sharing between groups. We develop formulas to ensure each subgroup trial meets specified criteria, comparing the new treatment to a control, by clinically relevant standards. For subgroups that don't meet these criteria, the method allows them to benefit from observations in similar groups. Notably, our approach uses a precise mathematical relationship to share information, unlike other methods that use simulated comparisons. We test this approach using simulated data, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing issues of negative results in basket trials.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed and high-accuracy. However, conventional control strategies often struggle to meet these requirements, particularly in motion systems that are susceptible to changes based on their position. This research introduces a cutting-edge modification to traditional control designs to address the performance limitations in these systems, effectively allowing for improved motion control even under dynamic conditions. The effectiveness of this innovative approach is showcased through simulation-based testing of a precise moving-magnet planar actuator, known to experience variations based on position during actuation and sensing.
