We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing numerical solutions for the n-body problem using high precision and order methods and established a data set for collision calculations based on the following measures: the time of collision occurrence, the minimum distance between bodies, and the total elapsed time before collisions happen. Initially, we discovered that the distribution of the first mentioned metric is not uniform but rather follows a singular, delta function-like pattern, which can be modeled using a Gaussian series (4). We also found that this metric's probability density function does not follow a traditional Gaussian distribution, instead requiring the symmetric skew normal distribution for accurate representation. We derived a theoretical expression for the probability density function of this metric, and through extensive data analysis, the derived expression closely matches the empirical distribution. We note that this derivation is significant because it does not rely on specific potential functions but rather is based on fundamental characteristics of motion. This derivation may potentially lead to novel findings in the field.

Measurements of the nuclear modification factors of J/$\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons were made in collisions of lead ions at the Large Hadron Collider. The study was based on data from both lead-lead and proton-proton collisions. The lead-lead data showed that prompt $\psi$(2S) mesons are suppressed, while J/$\psi$ mesons experience some suppression at high transverse momentum levels. The suppression of both mesons is more pronounced in the forward direction of the collisions. The study also found that suppression does not change with rapidity, but does change with transverse momentum level. Furthermore, the study found that nuclear modification factors for J/$\psi$ mesons experience some suppression in 0-30% and 100-110% centrality classes, but not in 30-100% centrality classes. Meanwhile, $\psi$(2S) mesons experience suppression in all studied centrality classes.

We propose an arrangement of predicates in continuous logic such that the
logical framework's meaning can be structured within a hyperdoctrine framework.
This hyperdoctrine can be incorporated into a hyperdoctrine representing subobjects within a suitable category of topological structures. 
To achieve this incorporation, we first simplify the hyperdoctrine framework for continuous logic and establish an equivalence between its category of equivalence relations and that of complete metric spaces under uniform mappings.

When designing a software system, even minor changes can have far-reaching effects, requiring comprehensive testing to ensure its stability. However, conducting tests for all possible system configurations is impractical due to time constraints and limited resources. This problem is complicated by the vast number of test cases, making traditional approaches infeasible. This research aims to address this challenge by introducing an efficient algorithm that identifies the most relevant test cases for a given system configuration. This test case selection algorithm utilizes singular value decomposition (SVD) and operates within the framework of the ParaSVD distributed computing system, specifically designed for large-scale scientific calculations. By integrating the algorithm into the ParaSVD test suite, we evaluated its performance and compared it to traditional approaches, demonstrating improved results in terms of execution time and resource usage.

Suicidal ideation (SI) serves as an essential indicator for treating and preventing mental health issues. Current methods for identifying SI employ single-source data inputs such as text from mental health discussions or detailed questionnaires from clinical studies. We suggest gathering and combining multiple data sources - mental health discussions on the Internet and clinical studies - to enhance the prediction performance of suicidal ideation. Given the dynamic nature of SI, which can change significantly over time, we also propose using sequential models that can process temporal data. We conduct experiments with state-of-the-art language models and a novel classification task designed to identify SI, which shows that combining data sources improves performance. We further validate our approach by creating a unique dataset for fine-grained SI classification.

Our research reports a significant 4.4 to 4.7 sigma detection of polarization within X-rays emitted from Cassiopeia A, a supernova remnant. Data collected by the X-ray polarimeter, IXPE, on 322, 350, and 377 kilosecond intervals showed cross-correlation values of 9.6 percent, 9.1 percent, and 9.4 percent with an average of 9.3 percent at 5.1 sigma significance. Three spin orientations were identified at energies of 5.0 keV, 5.5 keV, and 6.5 keV. Our findings support a two-component model consisting of a synchrotron radiation and a meson decay part. We observed that the strong polarization within the 5 to 6.5 keV range is likely to come from electrons in magnetic fields that have uniform direction, whereas the origin of the polarization within the 2 to 5 keV range is attributed to electrons that have undergone significant scattering in all directions. Confirmation of our results is needed through other observations and theoretical models.

Consider a set $\{a_1, \ldots, a_n\}$ of distinct positive integers where $a_1 < \ldots < a_n$, with the requirement that only subset sums up to a size of at most $\lambda n$ be unique. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are still unknown and pose an ongoing area of research.  In this study, we investigate dense matter properties in the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, with the addition of strange mesons and constant baryon chemical potential.  In lab experiments, it is possible to create dense matter similar to this under specific conditions.  In this investigation, we focus on the fundamental sound wave velocity, examining its relationship with density, angular momentum, and magnetic field strength for diverse nuclear force parameters and variations in electron and muon density.  In dense matter, the sound wave velocity determines how information travels in dense matter and, in fourth-order parameterized theories of gravitational waves, affects the gradient of gravitational potential.  In neutron stars, sound wave velocities can reveal details about material composition, whereas in neutron rich matter, it can be created in heavy-ion collisions and applied to the study of compact stars.  In particular, we discovered that, in dense matter, a higher degree of isotopic nucleon nucleon interaction results in lower sound wave velocity compared to symmetric nucleon nucleon interactions.  Additionally, in dense matter, the presence of muons leads to lower sound wave velocity compared to situations with no muons present.  In dense matter, a magnetic field can cause sound wave velocity to decrease or increase based on specific matter properties.

We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance could offer a valuable advantage.

During gas-liquid interfaces that are subject to irregular movement such as splashing and atomization, the resulting fluid structures can be intricate and embedded in their surroundings. In this work, we employ a technique called skeletonization to extract the fundamental information needed to represent their geometry. By applying a modified version of a previous approach that efficiently captures the dynamics of multi-component flows with distinct interfaces, we successfully simplify the representation of a periodic liquid jet. This involves propagating a gradient through the structure and simultaneously adjusting its interfaces, ultimately leading to their convergence into the essential framework of the jet's morphology. This framework, which represents the fundamental structure of the jet, is coupled with a quantitative assessment of the interfaces' deviation from the framework. Furthermore, we introduce a concept called topological number to quantify the branches of the structure, which serves as a crucial evaluation metric for evaluating the methods used to extract the framework. In this study, this metric reveals that the proposed modification not only enhances the representation of the jet's morphology but also outperforms the existing approach in capturing its branching topology.

Researchers discovered that certain influenza viruses exhibit active movement on surfaces with carbohydrate layers, contrary to expectations. They found that the rolling motion arises due to the interaction of viral envelopes with sugars, which causes them to bend and move. By applying principles of elasticity and fluid dynamics, the team created a model to study this phenomenon. Based on this framework, the team analyzed the effect of distinct viral shapes, surface layers, and carbohydrate interactions on movement. Their simulation showed that A/H1N1 viruses move by rolling due to the flexibility of their spikes, whereas SARS-CoV-2 viruses do not exhibit the same level of movement. Interestingly, altering the carbohydrate interactions or changing the viral shapes could make SARS-CoV-2 viruses move as well. Studying viral movement could provide insights into virus transmission and infection processes, and potentially lead to the development of new countermeasures.

We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Compounds composed of potassium ($A=$ K, Rb, Cs) combined with boron in a 2:1 ratio, exhibit unique cubic structures called the Laves phase with a specific Fd$\bar{3}$m symmetry. The arrangement of atoms within this phase leads to restricted vibrational motion. Theory suggests that this phase can support chiral phonons, which have distinct forms based on inversion symmetry. By analyzing the phonon properties, it was found that this phase can support both radial and hollow phonons with chiral characteristics. The results were further validated through experimental measurement of the Raman scattering spectra, which demonstrates the presence of chiral phonons in this phase.

In insulators, Born effective charges relate to how the positioning of individual atomic sublattices generates electric polarization, a concept seemingly unrelated to metals. However, our findings reveal that, when treated nonadiabatically, each atomic sublattice in metals can contribute to polarization, and the corresponding Born effective charges exhibit continuity from insulating to metallic states. We demonstrate that the large polarization in metals (evaluated over a small volume) arises from rapid oscillations of valence electrons, consistent with the Landau's duality principle. These polarization contributions automatically apply to magnetic systems, including materials like bismuth with multiple charge sublattices.

We are reassessing the significance of thermal fluctuations in incompressible fluid turbulence and determining their role in dissipating energy. By applying the framework of the refined similarity theory to the energy spectrum $E(k,t)$, we find that the spectrum of instantaneous fluctuations ${\sigma^2(k)}$ decreases at a rate of $k^{-2}$ in three-dimensional turbulence. This rate is supported by direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations under decaying isotropic turbulence. As a result, we find that the average energy dissipation rate per unit volume is equal to twice the average kinetic energy per unit volume divided by the turbulent timescale, which is consistent with the refined similarity theory. This result implies that the fraction of kinetic energy dissipated per unit time is very small, on the order of $(\nu \overline{u})^2 / \overline{u}^2$. Consequently, we conclude that the incompressible fluid turbulence regime is generally non-equilibrium in nature.

Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by their magnetoelectric properties. We are exploring the physical implications of a novel aspect of this phenomenon, where a magnetic field's presence or absence influences the electron spin's orbital movement in a non-linear manner. This investigation covers various scenarios, such as the time-reversal symmetry breaking of a Witten type, occurring in the presence of a Zeeman field and external potential, as well as under conditions that violate time-reversal symmetry, resulting in anomalous behavior related to the chiral magnetic effect. We show that the time-reversal symmetry breaking of a Witten type can be equivalent to a fractional quantum Hall effect that involves half-integer values. Additionally, we examine the magnetoelectric properties within the framework of a Chern insulator, using a gate voltage that modulates the electron spin's orbital movement in a time-reversal symmetry compatible way.

In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's map exhibits mode locking, characteristic of laminar chaos. For the first time, we establish a link between Arnold tongue patterns in parameter space and the diffusive behavior of delay systems. Contrary to expectation, this increase in diffusion is accompanied by a considerable decrease in the system's effective dimensionality.

We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient denotational and operational interpretations of the stochastic lambda calculus. By adapting established techniques to reason about high-level probabilistic code, this study achieves a breakthrough in linking operational and denotational views with a proven adequacy theorem, thereby closing a key outstanding issue identified in earlier work (Bacci et al., 2018).

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are beneficial to label as relevant to software design for documentation and improvement purposes. This is made possible through a process called design mining, which applies machine learning to categorize discussions as pertaining to design. This paper showcases a simple model for design mining, revealing that current methods suffer from inconsistent conclusions on various discussion types and projects. We then introduce and demonstrate two effective techniques - data enrichment and project adaptation - that enhance design mining's reliability and adaptability across different datasets, achieving stable classification results in both cases.

A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of a superfluid. Gravity emerges from topological defects within the post-inflationary macro-quantum coherent holographic vacuum state. Notably, this model successfully predicts the order of magnitude of dark energy and dark matter in the universe.

Proximal methods can efficiently uncover the underlying pattern in nonsmooth optimization problems, and, in many cases, identifying this structure is a free byproduct, also enhancing the convergence rate once aligned with that of the problem's optimal solution. Nonetheless, pinpointing the exact structure is not possible without adaptation. By integrating second-order information from the proximal gradient method, we introduce a novel algorithm called the aligned Newton method, which takes advantage of the proximal gradient's directional information to refine steps, especially beneficial when the alignment improves, as seen in problems with convex-quadratic structures. Moreover, we demonstrate that, in certain conditions, the new method converges at the same rate as standard Newton method.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it follows that either the product of $a$ and $b$ is in $I$, or $c$ is in $I$. Our research presents numerous results regarding the characteristics and examples of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. It has been proven that if $I$ is a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ where the product of three non-zero ideals is completely contained in $I$, it then holds that either the product of the first two ideals is completely contained in $I$, or the third ideal is completely contained in $I$. Additionally, it is demonstrated that if $I$ is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal in a ring $R$ but a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal, then $I^2 = 0$. Furthermore, the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within principal ideal domains and Dedekind domains have been determined

We present the latest findings from a study on the fully reconstructible decay process $B^0 \to \rho^-^- \ell^+ \nu_\ell$. This involves analyzing data from Belle II during 2019-2021, equivalent to 189.9 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity. Both the branching ratio and kinematic distribution of the quark combination $VV' \ell \nu$ were calculated and compared to theoretical predictions, finding good agreement. The branching ratio was determined to be (4.04 ± 0.32 ± 0.22 ± 0.09) × 10^-4, in line with the prior world average. This study marks the first to utilize a machine-learning approach to distinguish signal from background in this decay. Additionally, a new technique was employed to determine the quark combination by analyzing the hadronic phase using a neural network dedicated to semileptonic decays. This innovation led to enhanced background suppression and identification of signal in this complex process.

Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation analysis. We integrated photonic technology, specifically photonic WDM, into our design to tackle the complexities of spectroscopy. By using wavelength division multiplexing, our solution combines multiple spectrographic signals into a single optical fiber output, facilitating easy detection with high sensitivity. We marked the wavelengths using Fabry-Perot etalons or laser sources, and developed a new photonic technology-based approach for spectral mapping. Moreover, our research showcases a photonics-based alternative to traditional LPAS and reveals a feasible solution for implementing spectral cross-correlation analysis on a photonic device.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and optimizing combination therapies. This paper takes a comprehensive approach, offering a theoretical framework that can address these challenges through relational machine learning models. It provides key concepts, assesses existing model architectures, discusses relevant evaluation metrics, datasets, and testing protocols. Furthermore, it highlights significant potential applications and suggests vital research paths for the future in this field.

Several local authorities face challenges in deploying advanced automated
evaluation of road damage due to a lack of funding and technical capabilities.
Notwithstanding the variability in road conditions, due to factors like climate,
geology, and maintenance practices, deep learning models have shown potential
in detecting road damage. These deep learning models are particularly effective
when trained using high-quality images and accompanying damage labels. This
paper showcases that the road damage detection model can be effectively
transferred from one region to another, even across different continents. The
model's adaptability was tested on unique datasets from the United States,
Australia, and Mexico, yielding impressive results. The outcomes suggest that
this approach could significantly reduce the costs and complexities associated with
training separate models for different regions.

Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  The challenge lies in environments that are modeled as Markov Decision Processes, and current imitation algorithms often rely on access to expert demonstrations in the exact same format.  However, when expert demonstrations are available in a different format, known as a source domain, and need to be applied to a target domain with varying states and actions, the task becomes known as cross-domain imitation learning.  Typically, this issue can be overcome by establishing a connection, known as a mapping, between the two domains; however, ensuring the mapping's accuracy proves to be difficult.  The current solutions are either unable to guarantee accurate mappings or require the formulation of a new cost function, both of which can lead to the implementation of complex algorithms.  Our proposed method, known as CDM-I2O, overcomes these challenges by reversing the traditional approach of mapping by utilizing target domain transitions to generate source domain actions and states.  The efficacy of this method was tested across a variety of domain shift scenarios, such as cross-atomic imitation, where the source domain is trained on a cart-pole game and the target domain on a mountain car game, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approach, known as CDTT, by generating accurate source domain states and actions in the target domain without the need for additional domain information. A massive Population III protostar forms early in the universe and has a vast magnetic field that extends across its surrounding disk. We have modeled this phenomenon and found that the strength of the magnetic field has a significant impact on the development of a protostellar disk. We used computational simulations to analyze the interplay between the protostar and its surrounding disk, taking into account the amplification of magnetic fields through differential rotation. Our models reveal that a massive Population III protostar and its disk are engulfed by an intensely magnetized region, resulting from the amplification of the initial magnetic field. This phenomenon prevents the growth of solid particles, ultimately stopping the process of planet formation through accretion. As a result, even large planets cannot form in this environment.

Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in data mining. Our study transcripts the sequential process of finding association rules as a logical deduction. We show that the association algorithm can be viewed as implementing a non-cloning deduction procedure. We also prove that the minimum-size bases for association rules are in a specific binary format known as DNF (Disjunctive Normal Form).

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to court.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism by 17 percent over a five-year period following their conviction.  Interestingly, there was no substantial variation in crime reduction among those who received mental health treatment as part of their sentence versus those who received it without such an order; thus, forcing mental health treatment does not appear to enhance the crime-reducing impact of such orders.  Additionally, it was found that offenders who were given mental health treatment as part of their sentence had lower rates of incarceration and died fewer years after their conviction compared to those who were not required to undergo such treatment.

The authors of the paper delve into generalized Apostol-Bernoulli polynomials with parameters, derive their generating functions, examine key properties and relationships, and establish connections to other notable polynomials.

Radio maps serve as crucial planning documents, guiding wireless network service providers in installing access points and adjusting transmission parameters to ensure comprehensive network coverage. Creating these maps involves complex and time-consuming field work, requiring extensive knowledge of the area to select suitable locations. We introduce an innovative, efficient approach to estimate radio maps using autonomous unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Equipped with sensing capabilities and navigation systems, UAVs collect signal strength data while performing pre-determined flights along strategically planned routes. We develop and apply a mathematical model to analyze UAV sampling patterns and derive an algorithm to generate radio maps based on collected data. To assess our approach, we conduct comprehensive simulations and experiments in real-world settings, showcasing the efficiency and performance of our method.

This paper introduces a novel approach to identifying unusual behavior in time series data, specifically for systems that can be modeled using Hidden Markov Models. Our method assigns a likelihood score to each model state, indicating the likelihood of observing the data given the state's parameters. By standardizing these scores across various models, we can pinpoint data segments exhibiting significantly low likelihoods, marking them as anomalies. Our approach demonstrates satisfactory performance in detecting anomalies from real-world current-time series data and outperforms existing methods in certain aspects.

This research delves into a multi-aspect approach to person verification incorporating auditory, visual, and thermal modalities. Given the efficacy of auditory and visual modalities in everyday communication, combining them with consideration of thermal images, which capture unique characteristics in tropical environments, enhances system robustness across diverse settings. Our investigation involves analyzing three individual verification systems - auditory, visual, and thermal - as well as a comprehensive multimodal system combining all three modalities. Performance assessments were conducted using data from the NIST-28 dataset for primary comparisons and custom, label-driven data for secondary evaluations. Results show that a multimodal system outperforms individual modalities, demonstrating the significance of integrating multiple communication channels for reliable person verification.

Generating new training data through augmentation is achieved by appending existing examples to create new instances. We've found this approach to be both simple and cost-effective by using basic token manipulation such as removal, replacement, and combination. Applying this method to English speech data results in a 2.5% reduction in word error rate on the LibriSpeech test set. Similarly, translating English into Spanish using the ESPERanto dataset shows improved results with our augmentation technique, yielding a 0.2 BLEU score increase. Notably, our method also accelerates model training by utilizing a larger, augmented dataset. We've made our code available on GitHub at https://github.com/nyu-vlr/MakeMoreData.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_0$, using independent observations of $(Y_i, \theta_i)$ for $i = 1, \ldots, n$ where $Y_i$ follows $f(y|\theta_i)$. The observed data can be regarded as a finite number of observations from $G$ and this is denoted as $\hat{\eta}_n$. The goal is to find the maximum likelihood estimate that realizes the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ from the mixing distribution, making it possible to apply this method for sampling data. The paper applies this idea to estimate parameters such as the mean and variance. Theoretical results confirming the consistency and asymptotic normality of the estimator are provided. The method is also supported with simulations showing its advantages over alternative methods.

Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem. To address this challenge, researchers rely on Differential Privacy (DP) but its effectiveness is uncertain when data dependencies are present. Unlike independent data sets, the presence of data dependencies complicates the evaluation of DP guarantees. A recent study aimed to address this issue by developing a novel framework that determines the privacy breaches in one-sided DP settings. This framework considers a data owner who knows certain information but not all, with the data analyst being unaware of any information. It also establishes a metric to assess privacy breaches when data attributes are interdependent. This framework can be applied to various DP implementations, such as DP-Sync and DP-MEAN. We will demonstrate its application on the aggregation of numerical data and show that, in certain cases, the privacy breaches can reach up to 75%. Furthermore, we will examine the impact of data dependencies on the optimal DP mechanisms and explore ways to enhance DP robustness against data dependencies.

In protoplanetary disks, it is not uncommon to come across gas and dust emission substructures. Our investigation into the AS 209 gas disk used observations from the Molecules with ALMA at Planet-forming Scales (MAPS) project, which revealed a $^{12}$C$^{16}$O emission gap surrounded by a $^{12}$C$^{16}$O emission line that decreases towards the inner regions. We observed that the emission from chemical precursors, such as c-C$_{3}$S and CS, exhibits inverse correlations with the $^{12}$C$^{16}$O emission line. By modeling the synthetic emission spectra, we found that the outer CO emission layer could be composed of a low-mass envelope or a gas layer separated by a dust barrier. However, our models indicate that the gas layer scenario provides a more plausible explanation. Additionally, our analysis reveals a gas-grain chemical model that matches the observed CO emission intensity and spectral index. We found that the disk inner boundary's temperature significantly affects the CO emission spectral index but not its intensity. Notably, the observed CO emission gap and the low CO emission intensity at the disk inner regions could be attributed to the desorption of icy CO grains at the disk inner boundary turning into a gaseous state or to the processing of CO by organic radicals, which could lead to the depletion of carbon-rich molecules and, in turn, the depletion of CO itself.

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency.

We prove the existence of'mild solutions' for a mean field game involving first-order controls with a constraint requiring state and control trajectories remain within a closed, bounded Euclidean space area. This outcome builds upon Theorem 2.1 in the reference book by Cardaliaguet et al. and accommodates controls with measure support, whereas the reference book's result focuses on controls with a finite number of dimensions.

Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit improved spatial alignment as expected in real, interconnected structures, contrary to earlier assumptions. Calculating the masses of these structures based on their radial velocity dispersion revealed that they are actually not gravitationally bound. Furthermore, we found that these structures' ages, when estimated using kinematic parameters, are significantly older than their estimated lifetimes, suggesting that these structures are actually not coeval. Lastly, we compared the metal content of these structures to that of the bulge and bulge streams, finding no statistically significant differences, which indicates that these structures are likely not connected to the Gaia-Enceladus-Sauron structure, a major source of stellar debris in the Milky Way's bulge. Overall, our findings indicate that these stellar structures are actually dispersed moving groups, exhibiting similar characteristics in the Milky Way's bulge region.

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward 'yes' or 'no' issue, but in reality, outfits can be moderately incompatible, gradating from largely compatible to entirely incompatible. To tackle this complexity, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORer (VICTOR), a groundbreaking model that distinguishes compatible from incompatible outfits. VICTOR leverages the power of pre-trained transformer languages, combined with a specialized layer to capture the intricate nature of visual compatibility. Before being fine-tuned on an outfit dataset, VICTOR is trained on a massive 8M fashion item collection, allowing it to grasp the core characteristics essential for resolving incompatibilities. We also develop a novel evaluation metric to quantify visual compatibility, offering a more nuanced assessment beyond basic binary outcomes. Our findings demonstrate that VICTOR achieves remarkable performance, surpassing current state-of-the-art models, and showcasing its potential for a wide range of applications in the fashion industry.

The framework of quantum resource theory has successfully approached problems in quantum information processing with advanced methodologies. Recently, the theory has been applied to optical quantum systems, leading to numerous innovations in understanding quantum phenomena. This article discusses the current advancements in resource theories related to quantum light, with a focus on generalized quantum field theory. It introduces key concepts, such as the theory's mathematical framework, optimization techniques, and multiple resource management. The article provides an overview of quantum field theory's development, with a discussion on its applications to continuous variable systems, bosonic channels, and infinite-dimensional systems. It examines the potential of resource theories to solve complex problems in optical quantum computing, such as quantum communication and computation, and highlights the challenges and limitations of these approaches.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

This study introduces a functional calculus tailored to a countable set of operators generating contraction strongly continuous semigroups. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators.

Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a scale of micrometers. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes thermodynamic instability. As a result, primordial black holes forming in the early stages of star formation may comprise a substantial portion of dark matter. If these black holes are stable over an extended period, they could account for all dark matter; otherwise, they may still contribute a significant fraction due to their prolonged existence. The dark matter hypothesis based on these black holes is further bolstered by the potential for matter creation events that could have occurred recently, possibly fueled by the limited availability of dark energy in our local universe.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the intersection of two timescales - the speed at which the particles reassemble and the speed at which the particles move away from the expanding surface. This understanding allows us to divide the breaking process into three distinct time periods, each dominated by different physical processes. In the first period, the particles form a stable pattern far away from the expanding surface and a'sea' of particles forms near the surface. In the second period, the particles start moving towards this new surface and form a layer in front. In the third period, the particles start to pull away from the expanding surface at different rates, leading to an uneven distribution of stress across the material. This ultimately causes it to break. Our findings are consistent with earlier research and provide a detailed explanation for the breaking patterns we observe.

The main challenge hindering the advancement of integrated gallium nitride electronics lies in its low hole mobility. However, this issue can be overcome by taking advantage of the strain that results from lattice matching GaN to certain II-IV nitride semiconductors. In this research, we employed a series of ab initio calculations to investigate the strain-induced effects on the hole mobility in GaN. Our predictions are supported by experimental data. We found that matching GaN to a hexagonal lattice can increase the hole mobility by as much as 140%, while matching it to a tetragonal lattice can result in a 60% improvement. To confirm the practical applicability of these findings, we performed device simulations.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  The new method leverages Gaussian Process regression to address several contaminants often found in real-world robot data.  The proposed algorithm results in a sparse model that facilitates online prediction.  We evaluated the method in a realistic underwater navigation task and found it to be more efficient than current techniques.  The results demonstrate that by utilizing GP inference with sparse observations, we can achieve near-theoretical performance with reduced training time.

We examine a type of surface called isothermic when described through the combination of the Gaussian curvature and the mean curvature of its curves. Specifically, we focus on a particular subclass known as meromorphically isothermic surfaces defined via a complex function called a Calapso curve. Given this Calapso curve, we can define both the Darboux and Calapso transforms of these surfaces. In our analysis, we investigate how these transforms preserve key geometric properties, particularly Fubini-type identities and the associativity of curvature functions. Additionally, we look at how these surfaces are related to minimal surfaces within a specific shape.

We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This property allows us to estimate $P$ uniformly using finite-rank operators even when $P$ is not compact. We also establish that kernel-based techniques outperform traditional parametric methods like Galerkin methods in terms of convergence. Moreover, this research offers a new perspective on conditional techniques from machine learning and contributions from statistical physics and theoretical computer science.

This paper builds upon recent studies by Kim-Kim on the $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the first kind. We define and examine the properties of $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated identities. We begin by expressing these numbers as a sum of products of $\lambda$-analogues of partial Stirling numbers and $\lambda$-analogues of signed Stirling numbers of the second kind. We then establish a recursive relationship for the former and derive a formula for the latter. We also introduce $\lambda$-analogues of $r$-Stirling numbers of the second kind and their associated identities, in addition to exploring other related phenomena.

The consideration of time elements in knowledge graph embeddings presents a chance to enhance performance in related areas, such as link prediction tasks. Current research often incorporates time factors into existing models by employing transformations like time-embbedding matrix-attention and dynamic updating mechanisms. This paper presents an alternative approach that uses static models to analyze temporal relationships in knowledge graphs, focusing on enhancing the representation of entity embeddings based on their historical interactions. Experimental results on a dataset derived from Freebase and DBpedia reveal that this strategy can result in a 2% increase in the overall MAME score compared to a model that doesn't take time into account. Additionally, the proposed method achieves comparable performance on a semantic matching task for question answering applications.

This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold significant value for ongoing research regarding infinite graphs and their associated C*-algebras. Moreover, this note specifically explores the implications of Bates' theorem for the characterization of strong shift equivalence by means of paths within the graphs themselves, rather than relying on K-theory computations. This approach allows for by-hand calculations of strong shift equivalence classifications.

In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a hot and magnetized QCD plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed, spatially-resolved visualizations of heavy quark dissociation, showcasing the impact of magnetic fields on the process. Moreover, we have identified significant alterations in the K* quark's dissociation pattern, highlighting its potential for experimental observation.

To effectively answer complex questions, large knowledge databases are necessary. Currently, there is a significant discrepancy between the knowledge stored in databases and what is asked in questions, as many questions require intricate reasoning to be answered. Our proposed method aims to bridge this gap by integrating a knowledge graph database and a language model to enable them to draw inferences and answer questions on their own. Specifically, we train a language model to reason by generating question-answer pairs based on premises, and then guide it to find answers by using those premises as starting points. Our approach has been extensively tested on the LAMBADA dataset and outperforms baseline results, demonstrating strong performance.

We have developed a novel method of constructing high dimensional expanders by utilizing covering spaces of simplicial complexes. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available that offer arbitrarily small local spectral expansion.

Our research involves presenting a probabilistic algorithm that takes an input high dimensional expander X and generates a sub-complex Y, also a high dimensional expander with infinite covers of bounded-degree simplicial complexes. The generated Y preserves X's graph structure, reducing link complexity and inherits a sparsified form of X's links when the link size of X is O(log |X|). The basis of this algorithm is rooted in Lubotzky, Samuels, and Vishne's groups from 2005 that created the first constructions of high dimensional expanders.

Furthermore, applying our method to the lattices-based constructions of HEE, we have found a family of sparsified lattices that remain high dimensional expanders, offering a new dimension to the existing list-decodable PCPs constructions. The code thickness of these new lattices is merely logarithmic in the code size, a significant improvement over the current threshold of n^(1/4), where n represents the code size.

Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements.

We have computed the Benois $\mathscr{L}$-invariants for weight one cuspforms and their corresponding adjoint representations. Furthermore, our calculations extend Gross' $p$-adic regulator to non-critical Artin motives, which aligns with Deligne's conjecture on the L-function of motives.

Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve this issue, we have 
successfully integrated Rydberg atoms with deep learning algorithms, allowing the 
atoms to recognize multiple frequency signals simultaneously. In our latest 
experiment, we used a 93Rb atom transition and drove it with a 51 GHz bandwidth 
signal, comprising three frequencies: 4 GHz, 6 GHz, and 8 GHz. The Rydberg 
atoms were able to detect all three frequencies, which is in line with theoretical 
predictions. This breakthrough experiment opens up new possibilities for Rydberg 
atom applications in MW radiation, and may enable next-generation deep space 
networks and radar systems.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a significant HII region located in the outer rim of its disk. The galaxy's disk is composed of two distinct components - a stable system containing most of its mass and an active, star-forming interface with a separate kinetic entity. Due to the presence of a supersonic turbulent velocity field originating from gas losses during star formation, the outer star-forming disk exhibits high radial rotation rates, inconsistent mass models, and oscillating residual mass models. In contrast, the inner stable disk of UGC 8839 shows a consistent mass model, negligible tidal forces from a companion galaxy, and a stable, evolving potential structure.

For a quasiregular self-map in 3D space, research has demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of its fast escaping set can be any value within the range of 1 to 3. An estimated lower bound has also been proposed for the Hausdorff dimension of its Julia set under a specific growth constraint.

Using the Neutral Gas Ion Mass Spectrometer on board the Mars Atmospheric and Volatile Evolution/NASA Mars Science Laboratory mission, the CO$_{2}$ concentration in the upper atmosphere is measured. In partnership with the Mars Science Laboratory, three other missions, the Mars Global Surveyor, the Mars Odyssey, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, share similar observations of the CO$_{2}$ concentration. In the CO$_{2}$ concentration observations, the typical characteristics of gravity waves are detected, including amplitude, propagation direction, and phase speed. Three distinct source areas of the gravity waves are identified, located at latitudes of 0-10$^{\circ}$, 20-40$^{\circ}$, and 50-70$^{\circ}$. The upper boundary of the gravity waves is found to be around 140 km in altitude, and the largest propagation direction is towards the west. In the CO$_{2}$ concentration observations, the vertical propagation of the gravity waves is confirmed, and the highest stability is found when the distance between the source and the upper boundary is between 1000-2000 km. Moreover, the stability is only observed under specific atmospheric conditions, and it is found that the amplitude of the gravity waves gradually decreases as the distance from the source increases. In the CO$_{2}$ concentration observations, an association with the martian dust storms is detected, and the upper boundary of the gravity waves is found at a higher altitude during the

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an immense number of virtual photons, acting as "equivalent" photon sources. The ALICE detector, placed at the LHC, is poised to explore a broad spectrum of phenomena. Specifically, this research focuses on the forward production of the J/psi state in lead-lead ultra-peripheral collisions at 5.02 TeV. By examining exclusive processes, scientists can gain valuable insights into the gluon distribution within the lead nuclei, particularly at low Bjorken-x levels. The findings can be compared to theoretical calculations based on the rigorous saturation approach, elaborated within the framework of the Chern-Simons equation. The discovery of significant Pb--Pb cross-section differences relative to proton-proton collisions, combined with the investigation of energy dependence in collisions with larger relativistic speeds, are also key areas of investigation. The presented data include the measurement of the differential elastic J/psi and lead nucleus cross-section, as well as the examination of the coherence phenomenon manifested in the exponential decline of the cross-section at higher momentum transfers.

Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation have been impressive, but current models are limited by their reliance on specific training datasets and are easily deceived by minor distortions in the input visual cue. This leads to inaccurate and unreliable audio outputs, which may not reflect the intended sound at all. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework called the Visually Grounded Audio Generator (VGAG). VGAG incorporates additional inputs from the user, allowing for more controlled audio synthesis, while also incorporating a novel validation mechanism to ensure the generated sound matches the intended properties. By testing VGAG against the state-of-the-art audio generator, we find that it significantly outperforms it in both its ability to generate accurate audio outputs and its ability to do so on unlabelled data.

Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons, their variations, and expert tips for efficiently training fully recurrent neural networks, drawing from the Multiple Object Tracking module within our self-driving car project.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a delicate task, as modeling under specific economic assumptions often yields non-transferable results. This research investigates the effectiveness of timely countermeasures (imposing restrictions at the outset) in a broad economic framework, aiming to establish a universal solution that applies to any economic model. We analyze the trade-offs between health outcomes, economic losses, and countermeasure severity, defining a basic economic model that meets three essential criteria: (1) both health and economic metrics follow predictable patterns; (2) implementing non-pharmaceutical measures has a detectable influence on both; and (3) such measures can be applied uniformly across the population. Case studies utilizing realistic scenarios demonstrate that timely measures typically minimize overall harm, offering a potential solution to the complex pandemic control problem.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. Researchers have proposed various metrics to measure data reliability, but a unified framework is lacking to analyze the impact of uneven data quality across different groups. Our solution involves using the Shapley value to quantify the contribution of each data record to model performance, effective for small to medium datasets. We have developed a debugging tool that enables data providers to identify and fix data issues, and our experiments on real-world image classification and segmentation tasks have shown promising outcomes.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant transformation, where the distances between certain atoms in the material change significantly, stabilizing a helical magnetic ground state. Experiments have demonstrated that at pressures exceeding 1.5 GPa, the material's anomalous Hall effect is entirely eliminated. The pressure-dependent magnetization study revealed that as pressure increased, Mn$_3$Sn shifted from a conventional antiferromagnetic ground state to a helical state, where a required characteristic for the anomalous Hall effect is absent. X-ray diffraction experiments on a diamond anvil cell showed that this pressure range does not cause crystalline structure changes. The material's temperature dependence exhibits a distinct drop around 20K, hinting at an internal twist transition temperature. The material's electronic band structure, examined via high pressure Synchrotron X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, indicates significant changes at pressures exceeding 1.5GPa, aligning with theoretical predictions of increased energy levels displacement.

Formal knowledge acquisition is pivotal for developing artificial intelligence (AI)
capable of human-level cognition, with semantic relationships between entities being
one essential aspect of it. In the realm of Natural Language Processing (NLP), Relation
Extraction (RE), a subset of information extraction, plays a crucial role in acquiring
this vital knowledge automatically from natural language texts. By automatically
identifying semantic relationships between entities, RE contributes significantly to the
domain. Notably, recent studies have established Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) as the
prevalent approach for RE. In particular, the reliance on non-explicit learning methods
challenges researchers to define an extensive set of parameters, making transfer learning
attractive. This report aims to provide an overview of DNN-based RE methods.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where we apply a Robin boundary condition with a non-zero boundary value. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the spectrum. We also explore the behavior of the eigenvalues as $r$ tends to zero or infinity.

We investigate a widespread challenge in data analysis where we seek to reconstruct a complex network of interconnected objects from observed relationships. Our specific focus is on hypergraphs, which encompass various graphical models such as clusterings, social networks, and factor analysis. We develop a learning-based approach to identify the underlying hypergraph structure from partially observed data, achieving superior outcomes when compared to traditional methods. Our proposed framework allows for the incorporation of multiple theories, ultimately yielding a versatile hypergraph reconstruction method applicable to a broad range of scenarios.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document vital information about patients'
health conditions. Their findings are derived from analyzing raw imaging data and
describe the inner body structures. Preparing these reports necessitates medical
experts to be familiar with both normal anatomy and the detection of anomalies.
Current medical image analysis systems lack the knowledge of anatomical structure
appearance, making it challenging for them to accurately understand reports. To
overcome this limitation, we have developed an extensive dataset of chest X-Rays,
complete with detailed visual features and accompanying descriptions. By using
this data, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of using CNNs in identifying
relevant information in medical reports. We plan to make this dataset available
for public use to facilitate the advancement of medical radiology report analysis.

Bill Thurston initially found that Euler classes of taut foliations in hyperbolic 3-manifolds have a limited range and then made an educated guess that this range is the absolute minimum. Subsequent work by a different researcher, collaborating with David Gabai, found counterexamples that contradict this theory. Due to the connection between tight contact structures and taut foliations, researchers now consider the possibility that this theory could hold for tight contact structures, which are also related to Euler classes of one. To test this idea, recent findings show that previously found counterexamples are also related to tight contact structures, leaving room for the possibility that this theory might be correct for tight contact structures.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

Our findings provide concrete evidence for the stability of cryptocurrencies as a medium of exchange. Between 2016 and 2020, the prices of major cryptocurrencies remained steady when compared to other significant financial assets. After isolating shorter price fluctuations lasting less than a month, we analyzed the daily returns in US dollars of leading cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Ripple, alongside their respective counterparts – the Euro and Japanese yen, and major stock indexes, the S&P 500 and MSCI World Index. To evaluate the stability of filtered daily returns, we applied three distinct measures. Firstly, the Pearson correlation coefficients between the analyzed periods showed a notable increase in later years of our study. Secondly, the results of our dynamic time-warping analysis, which permits both leads and lags in relation analysis, demonstrated the existence of similarities in daily returns among cryptocurrencies and their comparators as far back as 2016. Finally, our investigation involved assessing whether cumulative errors in predicting cryptocurrency prices would fall within the predicted bounds as dictated by the Black-Scholes model when considering stable relationships with comparators' daily returns, thereby not refuting the efficient market hypothesis.

By integrating analytical methods including field theory, probability and integrability, we resolve the large deviation issue of the KPZ equation through solving the related weak noise theory. The noise's small magnitude allows for a Taylor expansion of the action functional, which is verified to be a Gaussian variant. The proof involves demonstrating the equivalence between solving this issue and integrating the Zakharov-Shabat system through the inverse scattering method.

The solar wind's compressive plasma turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed using data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission. Utilizing both the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and calibrated spacecraft potential measurements from the Spin Plane Double Probe, researchers are able to investigate turbulent patterns down to specific frequencies. These observations are made possible by developing a novel technique to determine the electric field spectral information in a precise and accurate manner. Data collected near the Sun's corona reveal that low-collisionality plasma turbulence characteristics are present, with a particular scale range exhibiting a power spectral index of about 3, in accordance with theoretical models. Additionally, it has been found that cross-power spectral analysis of perpendicular and parallel components shows shared indices across various intervals, indicating that these components are coherently related. These findings are consistent when considering differing cadidates of plasma frequencies.

In satchel undulators, the nonlinear resonance produces an electron beam with a tailored energy chirp, which is exploited to generate extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray free electrons using the SASE FEL technique. The desired output can be obtained by adjusting either the undulator magnetic field or the electron energy chopper, thereby eliminating the need for energy chirp modulation in these cases. A numerical study was conducted using the MAD-X simulator to examine two cases: modifying the undulator's inflection point and changing the energy chopper's profile. The results from these studies can provide insights for the hard X-ray free electron laser (FEL) facility at Diamond Light Source, which features an undulator with a 217.5 meter total length and an energy chirp taper system.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated, incorporating eddy coefficients that influence viscosity but neglect those affecting diffusivity. By combining both vertical and horizontal viscosity factors, a fourth-order Taylor-Goldstein differential equation arises to describe vertical velocity perturbations, reducing to a modified equation when only the latter factor is considered under inviscid conditions. Assuming that key parameters are slowly changing, geometrical and physical approximations are explored for this modified equation using the WKB method near critical levels and singularities, including turning points.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to enhance sensitivity to defects without losing relevant fabric pattern information. Since normal fabric patterns exhibit low-rank properties, low-rank decomposition is applied to identify anomalies. Our method involves constructing a fabric descriptor matrix for each image, performing SVD, and defining a threshold to determine the rank of the matrix. Any rank exceeding this threshold indicates the presence of defects. The method effectively detects defects, with experimental results indicating that fabric pattern recognition can be partially compromised but not completely eliminated to facilitate defect detection.

To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the system acquires actionable knowledge, effectively integrating short-term and long-term rewards. Through a variational autoencoder that predicts future visual content based on the agent's actions, the agent learns a generalized, actionable representation of its surroundings. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our proposed method achieves significant improvements in navigation performance, with an average boost of 10% compared to a system without this constraint, particularly in scenarios involving diverse navigation targets and varied action spaces.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III remnant clusters under the influence of an isothermal halo with $10^5$cubed kilometers in mass. Within a 100 parsec radius, a high-density nuclear cluster forms containing multiple Population III massive stars. We track the movement and interactions of these stars within the cluster as they evolve and apply principles of general relativity to model their individual paths and interactions. The simulation yields two primary outcomes: (i) the merger of Population III massive stars results in the creation of a black hole of 10 to 100 times the mass of our sun, rather than a black hole of 10^3 to 10^6 times the mass of our sun, indicating a less efficient merger process; (ii) as a nuclear cluster's stellar density decreases due to the evolution of its stars, the likelihood of future mergers of black holes within it increases, resulting in more massive black holes. When a black hole of 100 to 1000 times the mass of our sun exists within the nuclear cluster, it produces gravitational waves at frequencies of 1 to 100 Hertz, detectable by ARES and future gravitational wave detectors with greater sensitivity like LISA, with signal durations of 1 to 1000 seconds. These findings have implications for the efficiency of Population III remnant cluster formation in regulating the growth of massive black holes through stellar collisions.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies that focus on real-world scenarios involving ESS operations in different modes.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly driven by the $\omega$ meson. On the other hand, the cascade decays involving the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons are substantially suppressed compared to other diagrams, specifically those that go through the $\psi(2S)$ or a three-body decay of $\rho$. The measured branching ratios for these decays are as follows: $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma(\omega)$ = $(9.1\pm0.3)%$, $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma(\omega)$ = $(3.6\pm0.9)%$, $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma(\rho)$ = $(0.3\pm0.2)%$, and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma(\rho)$ = $(0.2\pm0.1)%$. The estimated width for the X(3872) decay into J/psi pi gamma through omega is about 3.5 MeV, while the X(3872) decay into J/psi pi pi gamma through omega is approximately 7

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform for measuring the capabilities of natural language processing systems. Traditional approaches struggle to process more than a few dozen steps per second, limiting their effectiveness in comprehensive training. We introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-performance simulator built using C++ that achieves an unprecedented one million steps per second, surpassing current benchmarks by a factor of one hundred. We evaluate its reliability through the analysis of 211 TextWorld levels at rates exceeding 40,000 steps per second, demonstrating comparable results to the original Python TextWorld.

The study on varying electron spin orientation employs the coordinate transformation method. Characteristically, Topological Insulators exhibit an uneven spin orientation shift when moving around the core. Nevertheless, the presence of defects within these systems introduces uncertainty, rendering the coordinate transformation method impractical. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel approach for evaluating spin orientation in systems containing flaws. By applying a special Nyquist frequency filter, referred to as the topological insulator passband, we can analyze the spin orientation behavior around the core of defects. Consequently, this approach enables the computation of the spin density within the core region. Moreover, this method can be extended to investigate higher-dimensional Topological Insulators.
